transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Li (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood Solutions), Maya Chen (CTO, Scoutline), Ethan Park (Lead ML Eng, Scoutline), Priya Singh (Infra), Noah Rivera (Product)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on whether Scoutline should use Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, or Private for their new real-time summarization product. Primary topics: p95 latency targets (<= 200ms token streaming goal), concurrency model (typical steady 150 concurrent streams, spikes to ~1,200 for 30s), streaming tokens/sec capacity, KV/prefix cache needs, and security (SOC2/KMS/SAML).

Topics discussed:
- p95 target 180-220ms for short-turn prompts (<= 32 tokens generated), 400ms acceptable for long turn (200 tokens)
- Streaming vs batch tradeoffs and how Redwood handles continuous batching and KV cache
- Hosted fallback and autoscale options vs Dedicated reserved pools and Private (VPC) – data residency and KMS needs
- Benchmark plan and pilot success criteria

Action items (from discussion): see action_items field above.

Transcript body:
[00:00:05] Samira: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we got about an hour, we'll try to cover hosting modes and the p ninety five targets you mentioned in the intake form.
[00:00:14] Maya: thanks, yeah appreciate it. we want to make sure we pick the right hosting mode up front because we have regulatory and latency constraints.
[00:00:20] Ethan: and we also have the product team pushing — they want streaming summarization realtime for calls, so tokens per second and sustained concurrency matter.
[00:00:29] Jonah: quick intro, i'm Jonah on the SE side, i'll try to keep the deep stuff concrete — kernel selection, batching, kv cache, that sort of thing.
[00:00:36] Priya: great. from infra perspective we run on GCP in us-east with a mix of internal services behind corporate SSO. we need SAML + SCIM and KMS for key management. SOC2 is required.
[00:00:46] Samira: noted. Redwood supports SAML and KMS integrations, and we have SOC2 docs — i'll share the security pack after this call.
[00:00:52] Noah: quick question — hosted is easiest but does it meet our latency SLOs?
[00:00:57] Jonah: that's the heart of it. so hosted can absolutely meet low p95 for many models if you pick the right model variant and region. the main levers are model size, quantization, and how much prefetch/prefix cache you can use. for streaming short responses — say 8-32 generated tokens — we've seen p95s in the 80-160ms range on optimized open models. that said, for heavy sustained concurrency with spikes, dedicated pools give you predictable throughput.
[00:01:28] Ethan: can you unpack "optimized open models" — are you talking about the rLLa family? which ones have that profile?
[00:01:35] Jonah: yes, rLLa-7B and rLLa-13B variants we've onboarded. we also have tuned kernels for some 13B quantized variants — basically a 4-bit quant profile with AVX/AMP kernels that reduces per-token CPU/GPU overhead. but synthetic numbers vary per prompt. we always recommend running a profiling pass on your actual prompts.
[00:01:54] [00:02:02] Speaker 1: mhm, so what's the difference between hosted and dedicated for our use-case?
[00:02:07] Samira: hosted = quick start, pay-as-you-go, we handle everything; dedicated = reserved GPU pool in region, higher throughput predictability, private = customer-controlled VPC and control plane. main tradeoff: cost and predictability vs operational overhead.
[00:02:22] Maya: our p95 target is 200 ms for the 90% of calls that are short; the product team will accept up to 400ms on long tails. concurrency is bot — typical steady 150, spikes up to 1.2k for 20-40 seconds during end-of-hour digest.
[00:02:38] Jonah: that's a classic burst profile; we have a couple strategies. 1) hosted with autoscaling + burst credits — decent but if you need hard SLOs during spikes, dedicated pools with burst capacity is safer. 2) you can use prefix caching for repeated opening prompts — that reduces token count. 3) route critical traffic to dedicated and background to hosted.
[00:02:58] Ethan: about prefix/KV cache — how big is the cache, do you maintain KV per session or per model? we've got long call history sometimes used as context.
[00:03:08] Jonah: we maintain kv cache per request stream session; prefix caching stores common prefixes at routing layer when safe (PII redaction considerations). cache size depends on model and memory; for 13B we typically keep 8-12GB of KV cache per model replica. if you have long histories, we recommend chunking and storing the embeddings externally and retrieving most-relevant chunks, lessening KV pressure.
[00:03:30] Priya: how about streaming token/sec — we need each stream to sustain at least 30 tokens/sec to feel realtime on mobile networks. can you guarantee that?
[00:03:38] Jonah: guarantees are tricky without a pilot, but typical per-replica throughput at 13B quantized is 120-200 tokens/sec in streaming mode. latency per token depends on seq length and batching window. if you need consistent 30 tokens/sec per stream at 1.2k concurrent, that's 36k tokens/sec across the cluster — approximately N GPUs depending on model and batching.
[00:04:00] Maya: ok can we get a rough sizing? like how many GPUs for steady 150 concurrency and occasional 1.2k burst for 30s?
[00:04:07] Jonah: rough back-of-envelope: for 13B quantized at 150 streams * 30 tokens/sec = 4.5k tokens/sec. one A100-style node (or equivalent optimized inference instance) can do ~8-12k tokens/sec in steady state depending on batch shape, so steady could be 1 node with headroom — but bursts to 36k would need autoscale to ~4 nodes. with dedicated reserved capacity you'd prebook 2 nodes + burst path to spin additional. these are rough — pilot profiling will tighten numbers.
[00:04:36] [00:04:40] Speaker 2: and what's the cost delta there?
[00:04:42] Samira: cost depends on model and hosting mode. hosted cost is usage-based; dedicated has committed monthly pricing with discount. we'll send a sheet showing example run-rate for the sizing Jonah just sketched.
[00:04:53] Ethan: when you say "burst path" does that mean cold starts? we can't have 2s cold starts during a call.
[00:05:00] Jonah: yes want to be explicit — spinning up new replicas has initialization time; for 30s spikes you'd configure reserved warm standby or use our burst credits which keep warm workers or route to a quantized lower-latency variant. we also support pre-warming policies that keep a minimal number of replicas ready. that's one place dedicated helps — you can guarantee warm capacity.
[00:05:18] Priya: for private deployment with VPC/on-prem — we have data-handling rules, and we'd like to keep raw audio and transcripts off vendor storage. is that achievable?
[00:05:26] Samira: absolutely, Private gives you a customer-managed control plane and optional on-prem runner. we can integrate with your KMS/HSM and the inference nodes can be placed in your VPC so logs and raw data never leave your network.
[00:05:37] Maya: what's required to run private? how long to set up?
[00:05:40] Jonah: usually 6-10 weeks for a standard private deployment including networking, KMS, and enterprise onboarding, maybe longer if air-gapped. minimal requirements: GPU nodes with NCCL support, Kubernetes (we support kube and also an appliance), and a secure control plane connection. we'll share a checklist.
[00:05:58] Noah: our compliance team will want SOC2 and detailed audit logs for the pilot. we need to see sample audit log formats.
[00:06:05] Samira: i'll attach our SOC2 report and sample audit log schema; we have audit events for token-level invocation, model version, route, and user id (redacted as needed).
[00:06:13] [00:06:18] Maya: ok, on quality — we may have regen/fallbacks if the model hallucinates. any built-in fallback to smaller/larger variants?
[00:06:25] Jonah: yes routing policies let you set fallbacks: e.g., if primary model fails latency SLO, route to a lower-cost quantized variant or a smaller model that is faster. that will change output quality, so we recommend a canary for 5-10% traffic to validate.
[00:06:38] Ethan: sample prompt set — i'll upload a repo of 50 typical calls and short prompts so you can profile. what format do you want?
[00:06:45] Jonah: CSV with prompt, expected tokens, and a few reference outputs is great. include average tokens generated and max tokens.
[00:06:51] Priya: auth — SAML with SCIM provisioning is mandatory for us. does Redwood support SCIM?
[00:06:56] Samira: yes we support SAML + SCIM provisioning; we'll add the integration guide link in the follow-up.
[00:07:02] [00:07:10] Speaker 1: how do you measure p95 on streaming responses? is it first-byte, last-byte, or per-token?
[00:07:15] Jonah: good question — we measure both first-byte latency and last-token completion. for streaming SLOs product teams often care about first-contentful-paint (first token) and p95 time-to-first-token, but for some features we care about p95 time-to-last-token. we'll align on which metric for your product — for Scoutline i'd expect time-to-first-token < 120ms for short responses.
[00:07:36] Maya: are there any known model variants that are particularly good at short-turn streaming?
[00:07:40] Jonah: generally smaller decoder-only models with optimized attention kernels excel. our rLLa-7B quantized low-latency path is a common recommendation for many streaming short-turn use cases.
[00:07:48] Ethan: what's the observability we get? we need token-level cost, per-route latency breakdowns, and tracing hooks.
[00:07:55] Samira: Redwood Console surfaces token-level costs, per-route p50/p95/p99, and tracing/trace-id passthrough so you can correlate application traces with model calls. we also have retention options and can stream logs to your SIEM.
[00:08:06] Noah: can we do A/B with different quantization profiles? we want to check quality erosion.
[00:08:10] Jonah: yes feature flags and rollout policies support A/B or canary; we can attach eval hooks and post-deployment regression alerts tied to your prompt sets.
[00:08:18] Maya: what about cold-start variability across regions? our users are global.
[00:08:23] Jonah: region-local replicas are best for user-proximate latency. cold starts will generally add hundreds of ms; we recommend having regional warm pools or rerouting to nearby region with failover policies.
[00:08:33] [00:08:38] Ethan: ok what would the pilot look like?
[00:08:42] Samira: typical pilot: 2-4 week technical pilot, you provide prompt set and traffic profile, we run profiling and give recommended config (model variant, replica counts, batching/latency window), then a short production-like run with your traffic to validate p95 and tokens/sec. deliverables: profiling CSVs, cost estimate, and configured staging environment.
[00:09:02] Maya: fine. success criteria: p95 <= 200ms first-token for 90% of short calls, and <= 400ms for long tails; streaming sustain >= 30 tokens/sec per stream; no PII leave our VPC for pilot.
[00:09:13] Samira: will capture that.
[00:09:16] Jonah: i'll prepare a lightweight profiler script; it runs locally and can be pointed at our hosted endpoint or your private pilot to measure tokens/sec and p95.
[00:09:24] Priya: one more infra nit — we want explanations of rate-limiting so product team can surface errors gracefully.
[00:09:29] Samira: we have quota + token-based rate-limits and graceful error codes; we'll include the error code map.
[00:09:35] [00:09:40] Noah: competitors — we're evaluating Anthropic too; they have a similar offering but unclear on per-token economics.
[00:09:45] Samira: understood. we'll include comparative notes but main thing is to run your prompts.
[00:09:50] Maya: ok let's recap next steps.
[00:09:53] Samira: recap: 1) Samira share pricing + SOC2 + audit logs + integration guide. 2) Jonah run initial profiler with your prompt set once you upload (Ethan). 3) Priya share concurrency/heatmap and SAML details. 4) schedule pilot kickoff week of 8/24.
[00:10:10] Ethan: i'll upload prompts to the repo by end of day tomorrow.
[00:10:15] Priya: will send heatmap and security contacts by Monday.
[00:10:18] Maya: thanks everyone, that was helpful.
[00:10:22] Samira: thanks team, we'll follow up with docs and the proposal.
